steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Context refers to the social, cultural, political and historical circumstances in which a film is produced and received, and which shape its meaning and significance.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Social context includes the attitudes, values, structures and issues of the society in which a film is made — class relations, gender roles, racial dynamics and family structures.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cultural context encompasses the shared beliefs, practices, traditions and media landscape that influence both filmmakers and audiences, including genre conventions and star images.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Political context involves the governmental systems, power structures, ideological debates and policy environments that affect what films are made and how they are received.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always connect contextual points to specific moments in the film — do not write about context generally without linking it to text. Identify the most relevant contextual factors for your film: not every context is equally significant for every film. Consider how the film's context of production differs from your context of reception — what has changed and what does that reveal? Use context to explain why certain choices were made: why this representation, this narrative structure, this visual style at this particular historical moment? Acknowledge that contexts overlap — social, political, cultural and historical factors interact and cannot be neatly separated.
